Coroutines and the event loop

Calling an async def function creates a coroutine object. await waits for an awaitable and can suspend the current task so other tasks can run. Use asyncio.run() as a normal script entry point. A notebook with an active event loop can typically use top-level await.

import asyncio

async def main():
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    print("Ready")

asyncio.run(main())
Example output
Ready

Run independent tasks together

TaskGroup schedules coroutines and waits for the group before leaving its block. A task failure generally cancels its sibling tasks. Prefer asynchronous I/O inside the event loop and keep CPU-heavy or blocking work away from it. Use try/finally for cleanup and let cancellation propagate.

import asyncio

async def read_source(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    return name

async def main():
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        sales = group.create_task(read_source("sales"))
        inventory = group.create_task(read_source("inventory"))
    print(sales.result(), inventory.result())

asyncio.run(main())
Example output
sales inventory
